name: Compounded semaglutide / microdosing GLP-1

lead: Compounded semaglutide has the same active ingredient as Ozempic or Wegovy but is prepared by a compounding pharmacy instead of the manufacturer. Microdosing means using less than the label amount, a practice seen in fat-loss and longevity circles, with the aim of lower appetite and body fat and a leaner face and physique with fewer side effects or lower cost.

Semaglutide activates GLP-1 receptors, which lowers appetite and slows stomach emptying. Approved semaglutide has strong trial results for weight loss at labeled doses. For microdosed or compounded versions, evidence is limited to a narrative review and early-stage registered trials.

paras: People get it from compounding pharmacies, often as multi-dose vials, and use amounts below the approved label. It is combined with diet changes and training, and results build over weeks to months.

Common effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety or effectiveness and has reported adverse events linked to dosing errors, off-label dosing, unapproved salt forms, improper shipping and counterfeit products.

chain: Lower body fat, leaner face and body
angle.text: Users take compounded or gray-market semaglutide, often at below-label amounts, to cut appetite and body fat for a leaner face and physique. Fat loss is established at approved doses in large trials, while the microdosing version has not been studied.

lead: Compounded semaglutide is semaglutide, the active ingredient in the approved drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus, that a compounding pharmacy has prepared as a custom product rather than the manufacturer's branded pen or tablet. "Microdosing" GLP-1 refers to an informal practice in which people use amounts smaller than the doses on the approved label, often drawn from multi-dose vials, with the stated aims of reducing appetite and body fat with fewer side effects or lower cost.[1]

In the United States the FDA listed Ozempic and Wegovy as being in shortage starting in August 2022, and federal law allows compounding pharmacies to prepare versions of drugs on the shortage list under certain conditions.[1] The FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety or effectiveness, and it has published warnings about dosing errors, doses above the approved label, unapproved salt forms of semaglutide, counterfeit products and products sold "for research purposes."

Semaglutide at approved doses has been studied in large randomized trials for diabetes and obesity. Evidence about microdosed regimens is limited to a narrative review and registered trials that are early or not yet reporting; no published controlled trial has established the effects of low-dose compounded semaglutide on appearance or body composition.[2][3][4]

Low-dose regimens for fat loss and appetite control

paras: Semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist: it stimulates glucose-dependent insulin release, suppresses glucagon and acts on appetite centers in the hypothalamus.[1] Approved versions are marketed as Ozempic (US approval in December 2017, for diabetes), Rybelsus (an oral tablet, September 2019) and Wegovy (for weight management, June 2021).[1]

A compounded product is made by a pharmacy for an individual prescription, usually as a vial of solution. Microdosing is not a regulatory category. In community use it describes using less than the labeled dose, sometimes also called a low-dose or maintenance approach.[2]

The FDA declared a shortage of Ozempic and Wegovy beginning in August 2022, and US compounding pharmacies may prepare versions of drugs on the shortage list if they meet certain conditions.[1] As of January 2026 the chief executive of Novo Nordisk cited up to 1.5 million US users of compounded GLP-1 drugs.[1]

The FDA states that compounded drugs should be used only when a patient's medical needs cannot be met by an approved drug, and that they should be prescribed by a clinician and filled by a state-licensed pharmacy. The agency says semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate are different active ingredients from those in approved drugs and that it knows of no lawful basis for their use in compounding. It also reports counterfeit Ozempic in the US supply chain and illegal online sales of products labeled "for research purposes."[1]

No completed controlled trial of compounded semaglutide or of microdosed GLP-1 regimens for appearance or body composition was found. A 2026 narrative review in Cureus summarized the rationale and reported benefits of GLP-1 microdosing across body systems, noting high demand and limited supply of approved GLP-1 drugs as a background factor.[2]

Registered trials include NCT07092605, an early phase 1 study of microdosed GLP-1 for health, quality of life and longevity measures (n = 150, enrolling by invitation, start date November 2024),[3] and NCT07588984, a planned cohort study of GLP-1 medication with behavioral health programs (n = 2,310, not yet recruiting).[4] Neither has published results in the sources reviewed.

For approved semaglutide, common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. They are mostly mild to moderate, dose-dependent and typically peak during dose escalation.[1] Rare events include gastroparesis and bowel obstruction.[1]

As of May 31, 2026 the FDA had received 990 adverse event reports for compounded semaglutide and over 730 for compounded tirzepatide, and notes that underreporting is likely and that causation is often unclear. The agency has received reports, some requiring hospitalization, linked to dosing errors by patients measuring their own doses and by clinicians miscalculating, and to doses above the label. It has also received complaints about products arriving warm, about multi-dose vial handling, and about labels naming pharmacies that do not exist. In October 2023 counterfeit Ozempic pens reportedly containing insulin were linked to hospitalizations in Europe.[1]

On looksmax-oriented forums, GLP-1 drugs are discussed as tools for rapid fat loss and facial leaning, and gray-market or compounded sources are discussed alongside approved ones. Users on one forum have described combining a GLP-1 with other agents during a cut before a lean bulk, and others have asked whether to add extended fasting on top of semaglutide.

lore.intro: Low-dose GLP-1 use is discussed in fat-loss and longevity circles as a way to get appetite suppression at lower cost or with fewer side effects, often alongside other compounds.
